blocks.text: No more acceptable is the view of the Chaldee translator, who held that in Ezech. XXVII, 15. the Hebrew word הבנים hobnim means peacocks, although R. Selomo follows it, and the other Hebrews are in doubt, and among our own scholars Pagninus rendered the whole passage thus: The sons of Dedan were thy merchants. Many isles were the merchandise of thy hand. They brought horns of ivory and peacocks as thy present. The Greeks (whom the Arab follows) and the Syrian seem to have misread this same word. For the former render τοῖς εἰσαγομένοις [tois eisagomenois], to those who are brought in, that is, הובאים; the latter לבונתא, frankincense, which in Hebrew would be לבנה. Thus of the ancients only Symmachus and Jerome saw that הובנים hobnim is ebony. Many things confirm this interpretation. [II, 715] First, hobnim and hebenus are not dissimilar words. In the first syllable the vowels O and E have been interchanged, which everyone knows to be frequent. Priscian, book 1: O passes into E, as tutor tutela, bonus bene, γόνυ [gony] genu, ποῦς [pous] pes. The ancients said compes for compos. In this we follow the Aeolians, for they say ἐδόντα [edonta] for ὀδόντα [odonta]. Quintilian, book 1, ch. 7: What shall I say of vortices and vorsus, and the rest of the same kind, which Scipio Africanus is said to have been the first to turn into the second letter, E. Hence the same people are called Ὀσσηνοὶ [Ossēnoi] and Ἐσσηνοί [Essēnoi]. And Ptolemy speaks of the Ὁρκύνιος δρυμὸς [Horkynios drymos], which others call Ἑρκύνιος [Herkynios], that is, the Hercynian forest. Second, קרנות שן והבננים, horns of ivory and ebony, are rightly joined in the Prophet as wares in some way homogeneous, although the one is obtained from an animal, the other from a tree. For, as Fuller notes in his Miscellanea, book 6, ch. 14, each has an extreme colour in the same degree of excellence: ivory, namely, of the most beautiful whiteness, ebony of the most splendid blackness. Both are highly polished, very lustrous, and remarkable for an incomparable smoothness. Hence they are applied to almost the same uses; and from both are made bows, combs, gaming boards, knife handles, etc. Third, the words of Ezekiel could be rendered thus: horns of (elephant) tooth and of ebony, in the genitive, so that the word קרנות, horns, belongs to both. For as ivory is called horn because of its resemblance to true horn, ebony too could be called horn by the same καταχρήσει [katachrēsei], since Dioscorides describes it as ἐμφερὴς κέρατι εἰργασμένῳ τῇ λειότητι [empherēs kerati eirgasmenō tē leiotēti], like polished horn in smoothness; and Isidore as a black wood, smooth and horn-like; and Avicenna as يشبه في ملاسته قرنا محكوكا وقيل مخروطا [yushbihu fī malāsatihi qarnan maḥkūkan wa-qīla makhrūṭan] resembling in its smoothness polished horn, or, as others say, horn worked smooth. Ebony therefore could be called horn καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs]. I would not, however, call it a tooth with Jerome, who has here teeth of ivory and of ebony. Fourth, ivory and ebony originate in the same places. [col. 141] For just as Polybius, Pliny, Philostratus, and, in the Scholiast on Pindar, Amyntianus in his book On Elephants distinguish elephants into Indian and Ethiopian, so Dioscorides, Pliny and Isidore report that ebony grows in India and Ethiopia. And as Theophrastus, Arrian and Ennodius mention Indian ebony specifically, so Herodotus, Diodorus, Mela, Avicenna and the Nubian Geographer mention Ethiopian. Lest you object to them these words of the supreme poet in Georgics book 2,

one must know that by the name India Ethiopia is also understood. Hence Servius on that passage: By India we understand the whole region of Ethiopia. That this is very true is shown by these words of the same poet on the Source of the Nile in Georgics book 4,

The river flowing down all the way from the dark-coloured Indians, [II, 716] that is, from innermost Ethiopia. There are some who add Egyptian ebony to the Indian and Ethiopian, as on the authority of Lucan, whose words in book 10 are:
— — — Mareotic ebony does not cover the vast doorposts. — — —

Maereotic, that is, from Mareotis, a part of Egypt near Alexandria, as they would have it. Consonant with them are these words of Servius: And yet ebony also grows in Egypt. But in both places there is an error. For in Lucan one must read Meroitica, as the distinguished Salmasius excellently proves in his work on Solinus; Meroë, which appears below in the same book of Lucan,
— — Meroë, fertile with black settlers, rich in the foliage of ebony. — — —
